title: Unequal treatment and administrative barriers restrict access to opportunities and support
source: Source: 2025 Multi-Country Survey on Socio-Economic Vulnerabilities of Roma. Quotes from the micro-narratives study.

content.content: Around 34 percent of Roma respondents experienced discrimination because of ethnicity, skin colour or language in the previous year, compared with 5 percent of nearby non-Roma respondents.

content.title: Discrimination on grounds of ethnicity, skin colour or language
content.subTitle: Previous year, all interviewed respondents. Each figure is one person in a hundred

sections.title: Discrimination also obstructs the search for work

content.content: Almost half of Roma respondents who sought work in the previous five years reported discrimination while doing so: 47 percent, compared with 10 percent of nearby non-Roma jobseekers.

content.title: Discrimination while seeking work
content.subTitle: Any ground, previous five years, among respondents who sought work

content.content: “For many years I have not been able to find a suitable job for myself… if somewhere there are good options, then they do not take me because I am Roma.”
content.author: Male, aged 30 to 49

sections.title: A nearby service can still be difficult to use

content.content:
The geographical analysis finds no substantial difference in travel time to employment offices, social welfare offices, banks or post offices between Roma and nearby non-Roma. Yet being able to reach a building does not settle whether someone can complete an application or obtain help.

The internet gap at home matters here too. Online information and applications are harder to use without a connection or practical help. In-person services remain essential for people who cannot complete these steps online.

content.title: Internet access at home for personal use
content.subTitle: All interviewed respondents

microViz.text: Cannot afford to have internet access at home for personal use

content.content: At the office itself, residence registration, recognition of documents and repeated visits to claim services can create further obstacles. One respondent describes the recurring expense:
“I feel discriminated against every year, every year I have to spend money on their bureaucracy and go from the village to the cities to pass all the commissions…”
content.author: Female, aged 30 to 49

content.content:
Each visit takes time and money from a household already managing work and care. Even making a complaint may leave the original problem unresolved.

Using the formal route does not always settle the matter either:
“My children are always bullied at school and in kindergarten… I contacted the human rights protection service, they gave me a warning, but the situation still has not changed.”
content.author: Female, aged 30 to 49
